dedupe_keys.name: port of houston and hurricane harvey 2017 disruption response and recovery unctad case study 14

description: This UNCTAD case study documents how Hurricane Harvey, a category 4 storm in August 2017, disrupted the Port of Houston and how the port and public agencies responded. The US Coast Guard closed several Gulf Coast ports including Houston on 25 August; the initial disruption lasted about two weeks, freight across modes was interrupted for more than a month, shoaling in terminals required dredging, and flooded roads caused congestion and driver shortages, while reconstruction projects lasted three to five years. The response included the port's hurricane procedure manual for staged shutdown, channel clearing by the US Army Corps of Engineers, up to 2 million dollars from the port for dredging, federal storm aid, and investment in hardened communications. It is case study 14 of the Resilient Maritime Logistics guidebook published by UN Trade and Development, which gathers 23 port disruption cases across regions with lessons and a risk management toolbox. Coverage: one port, 2017 to about 2022. Access: free web page; licence and cost: free to read under UNCTAD terms of use, with no open licence. Caveats: it is a narrative synthesis from secondary sources, figures such as total storm damage refer to the whole event, and there is no quantitative dataset. It supports emergency response and recovery planning for ports and resilience model calibration, and relates to the National Academies post-hurricane supply chain study and the UNCTADstat maritime transport data in the catalogue.
